title: Dynamic Programming — Policy Iteration & Value Iteration

questions.question: You can query P(s' | s, a) and R for every state-action pair of a small MDP. What is the most direct route to the optimal policy?
options: Run Q-learning until the return curve plateaus
Iterate the Bellman equation over the known model to convergence
Collect thousands of episodes and average the returns per state
Train a policy network with gradient ascent on the expected return over sampled episodes
questions.explanation: With a model in hand, sampling only adds variance to something you can compute. This is why the DP answer is what the sampling methods are measured against.

questions.question: What does value iteration collapse relative to policy iteration?
options: The inner evaluation loop — one max backup does both jobs
The discount factor, which it no longer needs
The transition model, which it estimates from samples instead
The greedy extraction step, which it performs during evaluation
questions.explanation: The max in the optimality backup performs improvement inline, so each sweep is cheap. The price is that it usually needs more sweeps than policy iteration needs outer iterations.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist on γ < 1 for the convergence guarantee?
options: It keeps rewards inside a numerically safe range
It makes the state space effectively finite
It makes the Bellman operator a γ-contraction in sup-norm
It stops the greedy policy from oscillating when two actions have equal Q-value
questions.explanation: Contraction is the entire argument: it delivers both uniqueness of V* and geometric convergence to it. Without it you need a finite horizon or an absorbing terminal instead.

questions.question: Your stopping test uses the average |V_new − V| over states and it fires while one state is still far off. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — average and max agree once you are near convergence
The guarantee is stated in sup-norm, so the test has to use the max
The tolerance should be relative to |V| rather than absolute
The average should be weighted by how often each state is visited
questions.explanation: A single lagging state hides easily behind a small average. The contraction bound only ever controls the largest per-state change.

questions.question: On a toy tabular MDP your Q-learning agent reports V(s_0) that is 30% off from what value iteration computes on the same model. What follows?
options: Value iteration needs a tighter tolerance
Nothing — Q-learning is off-policy, so a gap is expected
The two must be using different discount factors
Q-learning has a bug; DP defines the correct answer here
questions.explanation: On a tabular MDP with a known model the DP fixed point is ground truth by definition. That is precisely the debugging use the lesson recommends it for.

questions.question: Value iteration gives V*(0,0) = -6.43 on the 4×4 grid with slip probability 0.1, against -5.85 on the deterministic grid. Why is the slippery number worse?
options: Slips lengthen the expected path, and every step costs -1
The slip makes the process non-Markovian
The optimal policy is no longer greedy with respect to V*
The contraction factor shrinks once transitions become stochastic
questions.explanation: The reward is paid per step, so anything that raises the expected number of steps lowers the value. The operator is still a γ-contraction and the greedy policy is still optimal.
